title: Exact Analysis and Adaptive Optimization of Budget-Stopped Recycled Group Testing
content: Recycled incomplete-identification procedures test pooled samples through successive screening cycles. Negative pools are released to individual confirmatory testing, whereas positive pools are subdivided and tested again. The original exact analysis of recycled incomplete identification tracked the number of pools containing every possible contamination multiplicity, producing a high-dimensional unobservable Markov chain. Under independent unit contamination and perfect pooled tests, we show that this latent state can be replaced exactly by the observed number Pj of positive pools. Conditional on the current count, each positive pool produces a zero-truncated-binomial number of positive children, while cumulative tests and released units are pathwise functions of the positive-pool process. This yields explicit transition kernels, exact budget-stopped terminal laws, and a bivariate probability-generating-function recursion. We then study adaptive homogeneous policies in which the next common child-pool size is chosen after each cycle. Within this ELISA-history-only policy class, (m, r, R)—current pool size, positive-pool count, and remaining pooled-test budget—is a sufficient controlled state. We derive the Bellman equation, monotonicity and finite-budget-saturation results, and a sufficient condition under which voluntary stopping is suboptimal. At the original blood-bank prevalence, the adaptive policy improves on every fixed hierarchy in the stated 147-hierarchy comparison class for 37 of 70 tested budgets, with a largest expected-profit gain of about 242 per week. The reduction makes exact distributional analysis and adaptive optimization tractable without the rare-contamination approximation.
